newsitem.title: USA: Shippers welcome signs of detente in Conrail fight.
newsitem.headline: Shippers welcome signs of detente in Conrail fight.

text.p: Freight shippers, worried by the prospect of a single dominant rail network in the eastern U.S., welcomed signs of a potential compromise in the takeover battle for Conrail.

With Norfolk Southern Corp and CSX Corp at a virtual stalemate in their bitter fight to acquire Conrail, hopes grew that neither rail giant would come to monopolize freight transportation in the U.S. Northeast.

Late last week, both sides indicated they would be willing to hold a meeting to resolve the standoff, to the relief of shippers, ocean carriers, port officials and others troubled by the growing consolidation of U.S. rail freight, a $34 billion a year industry.

"It is definitely a step in the right direction, and a very necessary step," said Robert Voltman, director of policy for the National Industrial Transportation League, a trade group representing shippers.
While most analysts agreed that both Norfolk Southern and CSX would enter into the potential talks reluctant to cede anything, they said a compromise appeared all but inevitable.

"The only way the railroads of the East will be able to consolidate is if they can reach an agreement between themselves where they all feel it's pretty fair," said John Winner, a transportation consultant based in Washington, D.C.

If either railroad is to acquire Conrail, it will have to sell off a portion of Conrail's routes and grant significant track access rights in order to end the impasse and win the approval of U.S. regulators, he said.

Granting access rights to competitors helped ensure regulartoy approval of the Burlington Northern-Sante Fe Corp merger in 1995, and access rights and limited route sales built support for the Union Pacific -Southern Pacific link-up a year later.

Porter Wheeler, who was involved in the initial formation of Conrail in the late 1970s, said a negotiated settlement in which the "losing" railroad maintains signficant access in the Northeast would meet with far less opposition from both shippers and U.S. regulaors.
"Trackage rights alone are a rather weak offer, they need to control some of the lines," said Wheeler, a transportation economist with Bethesda, Maryland-based Apogee Research.
Without these concessions, shippers will do what they can to stop the merger from going through, said the Transportation League's Voltman.
"I suspect that Norfolk Southern and CSX will reach an agreement," Voltman said. "If we don't agree that that's the most competitive solution, we'll work to change it."

Either merger would create a virtually seamless rail network from Massachusetts to Florida, though CSX would reach farther south to Miami and Norfolk farther west to Kansas City. Without shared access, key points along these routes would be controlled by a single railroad.

Competition over routes is especially fierce in the battle for Conrail, analysts say, because it is the only major railroad that serves the commercial and industrial centers from New York City into New England.

"I would think that they would grant access and maybe sell a few pieces ... (but) they have to be careful about how much they chop up and sell outright," said Winner, who expects Conrail will eventually persuade its shareholders to okay the merger. "The network is more valuable as a whole than it is in pieces."

Among the most coveted portions of Conrail's network are lines stretching from New York City west to Buffalo, an east-west route through Pennsylvania, a Philadelphia-New York-Boston route, and a line along Lake Erie to Detroit.

The merger developments are being closely watched by officials at the Port of New York and New Jersey, the East Coast's biggest harbor. Port officials fear New York will lose business to its competitors in places like Halifax, Nova Scotia and Norfolk, Virginia, if a single railroad dominates transport along the East Coast.

Port officials have lobbied both publicly and behind the scenes to prevent that from happening. In December, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey issued a statement saying the merger represented "a historic opportunity" to end the virtual monopoly now held by Conrail.

If CSX and Norfolk Southern balk at a compromise, either of the mammoth railroads in the western U.S., Union Pacific or Burlington Northern, could seize the opportunity and make its own bid for Conrail, creating a trans-continental railroad. That prospect would not sit well with either Conrail contender, Winner said.
"They don't have much other choice," said Winner, the transportation consultant. "If they don't (reach a compromise), one of the western railroads will see that as a very good opportunity."
